about.title: The Americas I: Caral, the Olmec and Early Cities
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. There are six topics of roughly six or seven minutes each, with a short question after most ideas. There is a natural break after the Caral section (after the Caral 'built and found' timeline). If a learner wants to go slowly, split the class there and expect about 50 minutes in total.

say.text: Welcome. Today we visit two places in the Americas: the dry coast of Peru, and the Gulf Coast of Mexico.

show.text: The Americas I: Caral, the Olmec and Early Cities

say.text: Keep four places in mind: the Balsas River in Mexico, the Olmec Gulf Coast, Lake Titicaca, and Caral on Peru's coast.

show.text: Map of the Americas with four marked places: the Balsas River valley in Guerrero, Mexico; the Gulf Coast states of Veracruz and Tabasco; Lake Titicaca on the Peru-Bolivia border; and Caral, about 200 km north of Lima.

say.text: First, a big idea. An independent origin means a society grew its own farms, cities and rulers without copying another civilization.

show.text: Independent origin

say.text: Coastal Peru is counted as one of six places in the world where civilization arose on its own. That is why the Americas matter.

show.text: 6 places in the world where civilization arose independently (coastal Peru is one)

ask.right: A society developed farming, cities and rulers on its own, without copying another civilization.
wrong: It copied Egypt's pyramids and writing.
It began only after Europeans arrived.
ask.why: Independent means the ideas grew locally. The Americas are one of the few places where that happened.

say.text: The crops tell the same story. Each one was bred from a wild plant that grew right here in the Americas.

show.text: Mexico: wild teosinte grass became maize | Andes: wild potato plants became the potato

say.text: Now the crops that fed these societies. We start with maize.

show.text: Crops: maize, squash, beans, potatoes

say.text: Maize began as a wild grass called teosinte. Its ear is tiny, and each kernel sits in a tough shell.

show.text: A small, thin teosinte ear with a few hard kernels, beside a big modern maize cob.

say.text: Farmers in the Balsas River Valley, in today's Guerrero, Mexico, began picking the best plants about 9,000 years ago.

show.text: About 9,000 years ago: maize domestication begins

ask.q: About how long ago did farmers in Mexico begin to domesticate maize?
ask.why: Genetic and archaeological work points to about 9,000 years ago in the Balsas River region.

say.text: Maize then travelled south. It reached Panama about 7,800 years ago, and Peru about 6,700 years ago.

show.text: 9,000 years ago: Balsas River, Mexico | 7,800 years ago: Panama | 6,700 years ago: Peru

say.text: Squash came first of all. Farmers in Oaxaca, in southern Mexico, were growing it about 10,000 years ago.

show.text: Squash: about 10,000 years ago, Oaxaca

say.text: Beans and maize were tamed in separate steps. The whole set took perhaps 6,000 years or more.

show.text: Squash first | Maize in its own steps | Beans in their own steps | All spread over 6,000 years or more

say.text: Maize, beans and squash are called the Three Sisters. Grown together, they help keep nutrients in the soil.

show.text: Maize | Beans | Squash

ask.q: Which three crops are the 'Three Sisters'?
ask.why: Maize, beans and squash were the key staples of ancient Mesoamerica, and they work well planted together.

say.text: Now the Andes. Hunter-gatherers began domesticating wild potatoes around Lake Titicaca about 8,000 years ago.

show.text: About 8,000 years ago: potato domestication around Lake Titicaca

say.text: Andean farmers also dried potatoes into chuño. Chuño keeps for years and fed people through dry periods.

show.text: Chuño: dried potato that keeps for years

ask.right: Potatoes dried so they keep for years
ask.why: Chuño is dehydrated potato, a way to store food for dry times.

say.text: Put the dates side by side. Farming is thousands of years older than the first big monuments. San Lorenzo is an Olmec site we meet soon.

show.text: Roughly how many years ago? (approximate)

ask.q: Looking at the chart, which came first?
ask.right: Farming of squash, maize and potatoes began thousands of years before Caral was built.
wrong: Caral was built before any crops were farmed.
Maize was first farmed after the Olmec colossal heads were carved.
Potatoes and Caral are exactly the same age.
ask.why: The bars for squash, maize and potatoes are longer, so they are older than Caral and the Olmec.

say.text: Now to Peru. Norte Chico is a dry coastal region about 200 km north of Lima. Caral is its best-known site. Three rivers cross it: the Fortaleza, Pativilca and Supe.

show.text: Map of coastal Peru: the Norte Chico region north of Lima, with three rivers (Fortaleza, Pativilca, Supe) running from the Andes to the sea, and Caral marked in the Supe valley.

say.text: Radiocarbon dates show this society lasted more than 1,200 years, from about 3000 to 1800 BCE.

show.text: More than 1,200 years: about 3000 to 1800 BCE

say.text: Plainly: Caral was active when Egypt's pyramids were built. Sumer in Mesopotamia had arisen about a thousand years before.

show.text: Sumer arises | about 1,000 years later: Caral society arises, same era as the Egyptian pyramids | about 1800 BCE: Caral's era ends

ask.q: When did the Norte Chico civilization flourish?
ask.why: Radiocarbon dating puts its rise and fall from roughly 3000 to 1800 BCE.

say.text: Meet the site itself: Caral. It covers 626 hectares and has six large pyramid-shaped platforms.

show.text: Six large pyramid structures at Caral

say.text: The tallest temple is about 28 metres high. Plazas and ordinary houses stand around it.

show.text: 28 metres: the tallest temple at Caral

say.text: Many Norte Chico sites have a sunken circular plaza: a round open space dug below ground, about 20 to 40 metres across.

show.text: Sunken circular plaza

ask.q: What is a sunken circular plaza?
ask.right: A round open space set below ground level
ask.why: Sunken means dug below the ground. These plazas were about 20 to 40 metres across.

say.text: The pyramids and plazas show signs of ceremony. That points to a powerful shared religion.

show.text: A stepped stone platform with a round sunken plaza in front of it, on a desert terrace above a green river valley.

say.text: Workers carried stone in mesh bags woven from reeds and wild cane. The buildings were rebuilt again and again.

show.text: Workers hauling rocks in woven reed bags up a growing platform.

say.text: Trade held it together. Inland farmers grew cotton for fishing nets, and got fish such as anchovies in return.

show.text: Inland: cotton for nets | Coast: anchovies and shellfish

ask.q: What did inland Norte Chico farmers trade to the coast?
ask.why: Inland people grew cotton for nets, and in return received fish and shellfish.

say.text: Two things were missing. Norte Chico people made no pottery, and left no writing we can read. So we cannot know whether Caral had written laws.

show.text: No pottery | No writing we can read | Written laws: unknown

say.text: But a knotted cord, called a quipu, was found at Caral. The excavators think it was used to keep records.

show.text: Quipu: knotted cords, possibly for records

ask.right: A set of knotted cords that may have been used to keep records
ask.why: A quipu is a record-keeping system made of knots tied in rope. The excavators think Caral's was an early one.

say.text: Everyday life had music. Flutes made from condor and pelican bones were found, and people lived in houses beside the temples.

show.text: Houses and plazas | Flutes of condor and pelican bone | Elite who did not farm (Shady's view): priests, planners, architects

say.text: The dig found no weapons, walls or mutilated bodies. So Ruth Shady suggests a peaceful society. That is her reading.

show.text: No weapons found: Shady's reading

say.text: Caral was built about 5,000 years ago, but found much later. UNESCO says why it survived so well.

show.text: Caral is remarkably intact, largely because of its early abandonment and late discovery. (UNESCO)

say.text: Here is Caral twice. First built, about 3000 to 1800 BCE. Then found: Paul Kosok in 1948, and Ruth Shady's dig from 1994.

show.text: About 3000-1800 BCE: Caral built and used | 1948: Paul Kosok studies it; others doubt its age | October 1994: Ruth Shady begins systematic excavation | 2001: Science paper on dating Caral | 2004: Nature paper dates the wider region

ask.q: Who began systematic excavations at Caral in 1994?
ask.why: Kosok studied the site in 1948, but Shady began the systematic excavations in October 1994.

say.text: Now Mexico. The Olmec lived on the Gulf Coast, in Veracruz and Tabasco, between 1200 and 400 BCE.

show.text: Map of southern Mexico highlighting the Gulf Coast states of Veracruz and Tabasco, with San Lorenzo and La Venta marked.

say.text: The name Olmec comes from an Aztec word for this region, meaning 'place of rubber'. They arrived nearly two thousand years after Caral.

show.text: Olmec = 'place of rubber' (Aztec name)

say.text: San Lorenzo is the oldest known Olmec centre. It dates to about the 12th century BCE.

show.text: About 1200 BCE: San Lorenzo

say.text: It peaked from 1200 to 900 BCE. It sat safe from flooding and controlled local trade.

show.text: Peak: 1200-900 BCE | Safe from floods | Controlled local trade

say.text: San Lorenzo is famous for colossal heads: stone portraits up to about 9 feet, or 2.7 metres, tall.

show.text: Colossal Head 5 from San Lorenzo: a huge basalt head of a man with a flat nose, full cheeks and a helmet-like cap. Made 1200-900 BCE.

say.text: A head weighs around 20 tons. The basalt came from mountains tens of kilometres away, perhaps moved by raft.

show.text: About 20 tons per head; stone carried tens of kilometres

say.text: Many see the heads as portraits of rulers, because each face is different.

show.text: Colossal heads: portraits of rulers?

say.text: Next, La Venta. It began about 1100 BCE and rose to power after San Lorenzo declined.

show.text: About 1200-900 BCE: San Lorenzo at its peak | About 1100 BCE: La Venta begun | After 900 BCE: La Venta at its height | About 400 BCE: La Venta all but abandoned

say.text: La Venta's Great Pyramid is built almost entirely of clay and stands about 34 metres high. It is one of the earliest pyramids in Mesoamerica.

show.text: 34 metres: La Venta's clay Great Pyramid

wrong: They began in the same year
ask.why: San Lorenzo is the oldest known Olmec centre. La Venta rose after it declined.

say.text: Now these Olmec sites a second time: found. The heads have fascinated people since the mid-1800s. La Venta was uncovered in 1925.

show.text: Mid-1800s: colossal heads first fascinate scholars | 1925: Frans Blom uncovers La Venta | 1946: Colossal Head 5 found at San Lorenzo | 1955: Offering 4 found at La Venta

say.text: La Venta fell out of use around 400 BCE, so it stayed lost for over two thousand years.

show.text: La Venta: built about 1100 BCE; uncovered 1925

ask.q: In what year was La Venta uncovered by Frans Blom?
ask.why: 1948 and 1994 are Caral dates, and 1955 is when Offering 4 was found at La Venta.

say.text: The Olmec left no writing we can read. So art and buried offerings are how we learn what they believed.

show.text: No readable writing: use art and offerings

say.text: Olmec art blends human and animal features into supernatural beings. It links rulers with sacred power.

show.text: A small carving of a half-human, half-jaguar figure with a cleft in its head.

say.text: Jade carvings show an Olmec Maize God. The jade came from the Motagua River valley in Guatemala.

show.text: Jade celts carved with the Maize God | Jade from the Motagua valley, Guatemala | La Venta grew as jade flowed in

ask.q: Why do archaeologists rely on art and buried offerings to learn about Olmec beliefs?
ask.right: The Olmec left no writing we can read.
wrong: The Olmec wrote everything down but it was lost in a flood.
Colossal heads each carry a written story.
Because Caral's quipu explains the Olmec.
ask.why: With no readable writing, objects and images are the main evidence of belief.

say.text: La Venta was a sacred place, with few homes. It had buried offerings, such as floors of greenstone slabs, and Offering 4: sixteen small standing figures set with stone celts.

show.text: Sacred precinct, great plaza and Great Pyramid | Floors of greenstone slabs buried as offerings | Offering 4: sixteen figures with celts, found 1955

say.text: Olmec figurines from San Lorenzo show people playing a rubber-ball game. This is the Mesoamerican ballgame.

show.text: Mesoamerican ballgame

say.text: Rubber balls turned up at a ceremonial site near San Lorenzo. The oldest ballcourt found so far is on Mexico's Pacific coast.

show.text: Rubber balls on the Gulf Coast | Ballplayer figurines at San Lorenzo | Oldest known ballcourt: Pacific coast

say.text: Rubber balls were buried with offerings, so the game was tied to ritual. It later became part of how states worked.

show.text: Ballgame = sport + ritual

ask.q: Why are the Olmec linked to the start of the ballgame?
ask.right: Ballplayer figurines at San Lorenzo, and rubber balls at a ceremonial site in its realm.
wrong: The rules were carved on the colossal heads.
Olmec books describe the first match.
The oldest ballcourt ever found is at La Venta.
ask.why: The link rests on figurines and rubber balls. No formal ballcourt has been found in the Olmec heartland.

say.text: Olmec elite goods came from far away: jade, obsidian, serpentine, mica, rubber and feathers. Obsidian is volcanic glass.

show.text: Jade | Obsidian (volcanic glass) | Serpentine | Mica | Rubber | Feathers

say.text: Trade moved ideas too. Exchange networks spread beliefs and art styles as well as goods.

show.text: Trade carried goods and ideas

ask.q: What does jade at Olmec sites suggest?
wrong: Jade grew on the Olmec coast
ask.why: The most valued jade came from the Motagua valley in Guatemala, far from the Olmec heartland.

say.text: Everyday life: the fertile coast allowed two crops a year. People farmed, fished and hunted.

show.text: Two crops a year | Farming | Fishing | Hunting

say.text: Small figurines are often found in household rubbish and building fill. That hints they were part of ordinary home life.

show.text: A small clay Olmec figurine with a bald, elongated head, lying in a pit of household rubbish.

say.text: Let's compare. Caral and the Olmec were both early, both built monuments, and neither has writing we can read.

show.text: Caral: stone and earth pyramids, sunken circular plazas, cotton-for-fish trade, no pottery, knotted-cord quipu | Olmec: clay mounds and colossal basalt heads, jade and obsidian trade, ballgame, jaguar-human art

ask.q: Which feature belongs to Caral rather than the Olmec?
ask.right: Cotton-for-fish trade and sunken circular plazas
ask.why: Cotton-for-fish trade and sunken plazas are Caral. Heads, jade and the ballgame belong to the Olmec.

say.text: To sum up: civilization arose on its own in the Americas, built on local crops, with pyramids, trade and ritual.

show.text: Independent origins | Maize, squash, beans, potatoes | Caral: about 3000-1800 BCE | Olmec: about 1200-400 BCE | Next class: Maya writing and the Andes

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Caral's society arose about a thousand years after Sumer in Mesopotamia, and at the time Egypt's pyramids were being built.

frame_of_reference.when: About 1200-900 BCE (San Lorenzo at its peak)
frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Olmec came nearly two thousand years after Caral. By then Norte Chico's rise and fall, from about 3000 to 1800 BCE, was already long over.

other_side.claim: Caral is the oldest city in the Americas.
other_side.other_view: UNESCO calls the Supe Valley the earliest known manifestation of civilisation in the Americas, but the claim has been challenged. A plaza at nearby Sechin Bajo is dated to about 3500 BCE, and other ancient sites near Caral have been found.

other_side.claim: Norte Chico grew up around farming.
other_side.other_view: Early reports stressed cotton and fish, and the lack of a staple grain. Some archaeologists propose a 'maritime hypothesis', in which rich sea resources let coastal societies thrive before irrigated farming. A later study reported maize starch and phytoliths in tested remains.
This is Ruth Shady's reading, based on finding no weapons, walls or mutilated bodies in the areas dug. It is an interpretation, and the evidence for it is the absence of such finds.

other_side.claim: The knotted cord at Caral is a quipu, and quipus may record language.
other_side.other_view: The excavators argue this. Sources say only that quipus may also have recorded language-like information, as writing does. It remains an open question rather than a settled fact.

other_side.claim: Maize was domesticated once, about 9,000 years ago, in the Balsas River region.
other_side.other_view: The Balsas origin is the widely accepted view. A genetic study found that maize later mixed with a highland teosinte, and that 15-25% of genes in existing maize come from that mixing. Another study found that the last stages of domestication happened more than once, in more than one place. A study of ancient skeletons suggests maize became a staple only about 4,000 years ago.

other_side.claim: The potato was first domesticated about 8,000 years ago.
other_side.other_view: Sources give different ranges. FAO says about 8,000 years ago, the Natural History Museum says as early as 7,000 years ago, and one review says 6,000 to 10,000 years ago.

other_side.claim: The colossal heads are portraits of rulers.
other_side.other_view: Many scholars read them as rulers. Britannica notes the helmet-like headgear may have been protective gear for the rubber-ball game. Sources also disagree on whether the basalt was local or imported over long distances.

other_side.claim: The Olmec were the 'mother culture' that started the ballgame and other Mesoamerican traditions.
other_side.other_view: Related forms elsewhere were often selectively adopted and locally reinterpreted. Evidence from Etlatongo, Oaxaca, suggests highland villagers also helped create the formal ballgame, which challenges the lowland-only picture.
